source_phrase: Audi, Jesu sacerdos magne, tu et amici tui, qui habitant coram te, quia viri portendentes sunt: ecce enim ego adducam servum meum Orientem.

proposed_english: Listen, Joshua the high priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are foreshadowing men: for look, I will bring My servant, the Rising.
proposed_note: Latin Orientem ("the Rising," also "the Dawn" or "the East") follows the Septuagint anatole where the Hebrew has tsemach ("Branch" or "Sprout"); viri portendentes ("foreshadowing men") means men who serve as a portent. Clem1598-USFX prints capitalized Orientem ('the Rising'); capitalization is subject to edition-wide policy.
editorial_question: Disputed OT messianic capital (Zechariah 3:8): Clem1598-USFX prints 'Orientem' rendered 'the Rising'. Flagged for human editorial policy.

source_phrase: et loqueris ad eum, dicens: Hæc ait Dominus exercituum, dicens: Ecce vir, Oriens nomen ejus, et subter eum orietur, et ædificabit templum Domino.
current_english: and you will speak to him, saying, 'This is what the Lord of hosts says: Look, a man, Rising is His name, and beneath Him He will rise, and He will build the temple for the Lord.
proposed_english: and you will speak to him, saying, 'This is what the Lord of hosts says: Look, a man, Rising is His name, and beneath Him He will rise, and He will build the temple for the Lord.
proposed_note: The Vulgate renders Hebrew "Branch" ("Tsemach") and its cognate verb as "Rising" ("Oriens") and "will rise" ("orietur"), following the Septuagint "Anatole" (cf. Luke 1:78). Capitalization of 'His'/'He' for 'a man, Rising is his/His name' is subject to edition-wide policy.
editorial_question: Disputed OT messianic capitals (Zechariah 6:12): current English capitalizes 'Rising' and 'His'/'He'. Flagged for human editorial policy.

source_phrase: Et ipse exstruet templum Domino: et ipse portabit gloriam, et sedebit, et dominabitur super solio suo: et erit sacerdos super solio suo, et consilium pacis erit inter illos duos.
current_english: And He Himself will construct the temple for the Lord; and He Himself will bear glory, and He will sit and rule upon His throne; and He will be a priest upon His throne, and a counsel of peace will be between those two.'
proposed_english: And He Himself will construct the temple for the Lord; and He Himself will bear glory, and He will sit and rule upon His throne; and He will be a priest upon His throne, and a counsel of peace will be between those two.'
proposed_note: Latin "et erit sacerdos super solio suo" may be read either as "He will be a priest upon His throne" (one figure holding both offices) or "a priest will be upon his throne" (pointing to the two figures in "between those two"). Capitalization of 'He'/'Himself'/'His' reflects messianic interpretation and is subject to edition-wide policy.
editorial_question: Disputed OT messianic capitals (Zechariah 6:13): current English capitalizes 'He'/'Himself'/'His'. Flagged for human editorial policy.

source_phrase: Exsulta satis, filia Sion; jubila, filia Jerusalem: ecce rex tuus veniet tibi justus, et salvator: ipse pauper, et ascendens super asinam et super pullum filium asinæ.
current_english: Exult greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem: look, your king will come to you, righteous and a savior; He Himself is poor, and riding on a female donkey and on a colt, the foal of a female donkey.
proposed_english: Exult greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem: look, your king will come to you, righteous and a savior; He Himself is poor, and riding on a female donkey and on a colt, the foal of a female donkey.
proposed_note: The Vulgate reads salvator ("a savior," active, matching the Septuagint) rather than the passive Hebrew "saved/victorious," translates "afflicted/humble" as pauper ("poor"), and reads the feminine asinam ("a female donkey") where the Hebrew has the masculine "donkey." Capitalization of 'He Himself' (for lowercase Latin ipse, referring to 'your king') is subject to edition-wide policy.
editorial_question: Disputed OT messianic capital (Zechariah 9:9): current English capitalizes 'He Himself' for 'your king'. Flagged for human editorial policy.

source_phrase: Et disperdam quadrigam ex Ephraim, et equum de Jerusalem, et dissipabitur arcus belli: et loquetur pacem gentibus, et potestas ejus a mari usque ad mare, et a fluminibus usque ad fines terræ.
current_english: And I will destroy the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war will be shattered; and He will speak peace to the nations, and His authority will be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth.
proposed_english: And I will destroy the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war will be shattered; and He will speak peace to the nations, and His authority will be from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth.
proposed_note: Capitalization of 'He'/'His' (referring to the king of 9:9) is subject to edition-wide policy.
editorial_question: Disputed OT messianic capitals (Zechariah 9:10): current English capitalizes 'He'/'His'. Flagged for human editorial policy.

source_phrase: Tu quoque in sanguine testamenti tui emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu in quo non est aqua.
current_english: You also, by the blood of Your covenant, have released Your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.
proposed_english: You also, by the blood of Your covenant, have released Your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.
proposed_note: Whereas the Hebrew has the first person ("I have set your prisoners free"), the Vulgate uses the second-person verb emisisti ("you have released"); the Latin does not name the one addressed. Capitalization of 'You'/'Your' takes the unnamed addressee of 9:11 as the king/Messiah rather than daughter Zion (feminine addressee in 9:9); subject to edition-wide policy.
editorial_question: Disputed OT referent capitals (Zechariah 9:11): current English capitalizes 'You'/'Your' despite the Latin not naming the addressee. Flagged for human editorial policy.

source_phrase: Et effundam super domum David et super habitatores Jerusalem spiritum gratiæ et precum: et aspicient ad me quem confixerunt, et plangent eum planctu quasi super unigenitum, et dolebunt super eum, ut doleri solet in morte primogeniti.
current_english: And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and of prayers; and they will look to Me, whom they have pierced, and they will mourn for Him with mourning as over an only-begotten son, and they will grieve over Him as one customarily grieves at the death of a firstborn.
proposed_english: And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and of prayers; and they will look to Me, whom they have pierced, and they will mourn for Him with mourning as over an only-begotten son, and they will grieve over Him as one customarily grieves at the death of a firstborn.
proposed_note: The Vulgate reads ut doleri solet in morte primogeniti ("as one customarily grieves at the death of a firstborn"), making "at the death of" explicit where the Hebrew reads "like bitter weeping over a firstborn." Capitalization of 'Him' (for lowercase Latin eum, following 'look to Me, whom they have pierced') reflects traditional messianic/divine-referent reading and is subject to edition-wide policy.
editorial_question: Disputed OT messianic capitals (Zechariah 12:10): current English capitalizes 'Him' twice after 'look to Me, whom they have pierced'. Flagged for human editorial policy.

source_phrase: Nonne unus fecit, et residuum spiritus ejus est? et quid unus quærit, nisi semen Dei? custodite ergo spiritum vestrum, et uxorem adolescentiæ tuæ noli despicere.
current_english: Did not One make them, and the remnant of the spirit is His? And what does the One seek, except the seed of God? Guard your spirit therefore, and do not despise the wife of your youth.
proposed_english: Did not One make them, and the remnant of the spirit is His? And what does the One seek, except the seed of God? Guard your spirit therefore, and do not despise the wife of your youth.
proposed_note: The grammar is notoriously difficult; the Vulgate literally asks "Did not One make [them], and the remnant of the spirit is His?" leaving the object of "make" (fecit) unexpressed. Capitalization of 'One'/'His' takes unus as referring to God (rather than Adam/Abraham or the married couple); subject to edition-wide policy.
editorial_question: Disputed OT referent capitals (Malachi 2:15): Latin 'unus' is lowercase; current English capitalizes 'One'/'His'. Flagged for human editorial policy.

source_phrase: Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, et præparabit viam ante faciem meam: et statim veniet ad templum suum Dominator quem vos quæritis, et angelus testamenti quem vos vultis. Ecce venit, dicit Dominus exercituum.
current_english: "Look, I am sending My messenger, and he will prepare the way before My face; and at once the Sovereign whom you seek will come to His temple, and the messenger of the covenant whom you desire. Look, He is coming," says the Lord of hosts.
proposed_english: "Look, I am sending My messenger, and he will prepare the way before My face; and at once the Sovereign whom you seek will come to His temple, and the messenger of the covenant whom you desire. Look, He is coming," says the Lord of hosts.
proposed_note: Clem1598-USFX prints capitalized Dominator ('the Sovereign'); capitalization of 'Sovereign', 'His', and 'He' (versus lowercase 'he' for My messenger) is subject to edition-wide policy.
editorial_question: Disputed OT messianic/divine capitals (Malachi 3:1): Clem1598-USFX prints 'Dominator'; current English capitalizes 'Sovereign', 'His', and 'He'. Flagged for human editorial policy.

source_phrase: pœnitentia ductus, retulit triginta argenteos
current_english: Then when Judas, who had handed Him over, saw that He had been condemned, he was moved by repentance and brought back the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and the elders,
proposed_english: Then when Judas, who had handed Him over, saw that He had been condemned, he was moved by repentance and brought back the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and the elders,
proposed_note: Latin 'pœnitentia ductus' ('moved by repentance' or 'moved by remorse/regret') uses the edition's standard noun for 'pœnitentia'; because the Latin noun spans both remorse and repentance, 'moved by remorse' is a widely held contextual alternative here (cf. Judges 21:6).
editorial_question: Rule 4 & Claude checklist item: add alternate-reading note for Judas's 'pœnitentia ductus' and queue doctrinally sensitive wording choice to human editor.

source_phrase: per fidem Jesu Christi
current_english: namely, the righteousness of God through the faith of Jesus Christ, to all and upon all who believe in Him; for there is no distinction,
proposed_english: namely, the righteousness of God through the faith of Jesus Christ, to all and upon all who believe in Him; for there is no distinction,
proposed_note: The Vulgate reads "in omnes et super omnes qui credunt in eum" ("to all and upon all who believe in Him"), including "upon all" and "in Him" which are absent from modern critical Greek texts. The genitive "fidem Jesu Christi" can be understood either objectively ("faith in Jesus Christ") or subjectively ("the faithfulness of Jesus Christ").
editorial_question: Rule 4 mandatory test case: 'the faith of Jesus Christ' preserves the Latin genitive ambiguity AND already has an explicit alternate-reading note (objective 'faith in' vs subjective 'faithfulness of'); flag for human editorial decision across editions.

source_phrase: qui est ex fide Jesu Christi
current_english: in the forbearance of God, for the demonstration of His righteousness at this time, so that He Himself may be righteous and may justify him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ.
proposed_english: in the forbearance of God, for the demonstration of His righteousness at this time, so that He Himself may be righteous and may justify him who is of the faith of Jesus Christ.
proposed_note: The Latin genitive 'ex fide Jesu Christi' literally reads 'of the faith of Jesus Christ' and can be understood either objectively ('faith in Jesus Christ') or subjectively ('the faithfulness of Jesus Christ').
editorial_question: Rule 4 mandatory test case: Rom 3:26 preserves 'the faith of Jesus Christ' but lacked the mandatory alternate-reading footnote; add note and flag for human editor.

source_phrase: nisi per fidem Jesu Christi ... ex fide Christi
current_english: Yet knowing that a man is not justified by works of the law, except through the faith of Jesus Christ, we also believe in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by the faith of Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified.
proposed_english: Yet knowing that a man is not justified by works of the law, except through the faith of Jesus Christ, we also believe in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by the faith of Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified.
proposed_note: Latin fidem Jesu Christi and fide Christi literally read "faith of [Jesus] Christ" (traditionally taken as objective genitive, "faith in Christ," though also debated as subjective, "faithfulness of Christ"); the Vulgate also uses present-tense credimus ("we believe") rather than the Greek aorist ("we believed").
editorial_question: Rule 4 mandatory test case: 'the faith of Jesus Christ' / 'the faith of Christ' preserves the Latin genitive ambiguity AND already has an explicit alternate-reading note; flag for human editorial decision across editions.

source_phrase: in fide vivo Filii Dei
current_english: And I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me. And what I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and handed Himself over for me.
proposed_english: And I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me. And what I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and handed Himself over for me.
proposed_note: The Latin genitive 'in fide ... Filii Dei' literally reads 'by the faith of the Son of God' and can be understood either objectively ('faith in the Son of God') or subjectively ('the faithfulness of the Son of God').
editorial_question: Rule 4 mandatory test case: Gal 2:20 preserves 'the faith of the Son of God' but lacked the mandatory alternate-reading footnote; add note and flag for human editor.

editorial_question: Confirm edition-wide policy on Latin genitive constructions with 'fides': Rom 3:22, 3:26, Gal 2:16, 2:20, 3:22, Phil 3:9, Jas 2:1, Rev 14:12 preserve the natural ambiguity 'the faith of ...' (with Rule 4 alternate-reading footnotes proposed for all 6 loci that previously lacked them), while Eph 3:12 currently renders 'per fidem ejus' as 'through faith in Him' (footnote proposed for 'through His faithfulness'). Decide whether to retain 'faith of' + footnote everywhere and whether Eph 3:12 should harmonize or keep 'faith in Him' with footnote.

topic: Bare 'spiritus' capitalization in Ezekiel and Isaiah 32:15 (Rule 4)
source_phrase: spiritus (unmodified, lowercase in Clem1598-USFX)
editorial_question: In Ezekiel 2:2, 3:12, 3:14, 3:24, 8:3, 11:1, 11:24, 43:5 and Isaiah 32:15, the Clementine Vulgate reads bare lowercase 'spiritus' (contrast Ezek 1:12, 1:20, 10:17 where current English renders lowercase 'spirit', and Ezek 11:5, 11:24b where Latin explicitly adds 'Domini'/'Dei'). Decide whether to keep capitalized 'the Spirit' with footnotes or adopt lowercase 'a spirit' / 'spirit' where unmodified.

topic: pœnitentia ductus ('led by repentance' vs. 'seized with remorse/regret')
source_phrase: pœnitentia ductus (Matt 27:3); pœnitentia ducti (Judg 21:6)
editorial_question: The Vulgate uses the identical idiom 'pœnitentia ductus/ducti' in Matt 27:3 (Judas) and Judg 21:6 (Israel). Current English renders 'moved by remorse' (Matt 27:3) and 'moved with remorse' (Judg 21:6) rather than literal 'led by repentance'. Pass 1 preserves current wording and verifies/adds Rule 4 notes explaining the shared Latin idiom 'pœnitentia' (which covers both remorse and repentance). Confirm whether 'remorse' with note or literal 'repentance' is preferred.

source_phrase: christum ducem / christus (Dan 9:25-26); sanctum tuum (Ps 15:10); Justum / Salvatorem (Isa); etc.
editorial_question: 50 verse-level proposals flag OT Messianic capitalization where the Latin text either uses lowercase (e.g., Dan 9:25-26 'christum ducem' / 'christus', Ps 15:10 'sanctum tuum', Lam 4:20 'christus Dominus', Jer 23:5-6, Zech 3:8, 6:12) or capitalizes traditional Vulgate Christological titles (e.g., Isa 24:16, 41:2, 41:10 'Justus', 45:8 'Salvatorem', Hag 2:8 'Desideratus'). Pass 1 retains existing English text and attaches explanatory notes without silently forcing interpretive choices; human editor to set uniform edition policy.

editorial_question: Clem1598-USFX prints capitalized 'Deus hujus sæculi' (reflecting patristic ambiguity over whether 'Deus' is subject with 'hujus sæculi' modifying 'infidelium' or refers to Satan as 'the god of this age'). editorial_question: All Sixto-Clementine witnesses (Clem1598-USFX, Sixtine 1590, Hetzenauer 1906, Conte 2009) unanimously print 'Prosperans' ('making haste' in Late Latin / literally 'prospering', an old graphic variant of 'properans' = 'hastening'). Confirm translating 'hastening' with a textual note vs. strictly 'prospering'.

Confirm keeping this convention vs. closing and reopening quotes at every chapter boundary (flagged for Pass 3 & human policy).

Confirm retention of 'Mount Sion' (Deut 4:48, with clarifying note distinguishing from Jerusalem's Zion), 'Artaxerxes' in Esther 11-16 (reflecting Latin 'Artaxerxes' vs. canonical 'Assuerus' -> 'Ahasuerus'), and standardized spellings for Helon/Aijalon/Shemaiah/Echi.
